note: The session player steps out front. Purdie's own record is the clearest statement of a drummer treating groove as authorship rather than service.
listen_for: Ghost notes buried at the edge of audibility, doing most of the emotional work.
connections: Steely Dan - Aja; Aretha Franklin - Young, Gifted and Black

note: Purdie as musical director, and "Rock Steady" as proof that a rhythm arrangement can be the composition.
listen_for: The way the hi-hat leans back while the bass drum pushes forward.

note: The JB rhythm section at its most patient: a groove that refuses to develop because development would ruin it.
listen_for: Jabo Starks holding one figure for nine minutes without decay.
connections: A Tribe Called Quest - The Low End Theory

note: New Orleans second-line logic dropped into a CTI jazz-funk session, with Bob James and Joe Beck.
listen_for: Snare accents landing a hair away from where you expect them.

note: The opposite pole: technique as spectacle, and the record that made fusion drumming a headline act.
listen_for: The tuned-tom cascades in "Quadrant 4" and the sheer volume of information.

note: Jazz musicians choosing the groove over the changes, with Harvey Mason building a beat you can loop.
listen_for: "Chameleon" arriving as a rhythm bed before it is a tune.

note: Form dissolved into rhythm. The most influential badly-reviewed record in this entire lineage.
listen_for: Drums and percussion layered until the pulse becomes weather.

note: Zigaboo Modeliste's syncopation is the definition of playing less and meaning more.
listen_for: The gaps. Almost every important event happens in a hole.

note: Tony Allen distributes the beat so evenly across the kit that the groove stops needing a downbeat.
listen_for: Hi-hat and snare conversing while the bass drum stays deliberately vague.
connections: Tony Allen & Hugh Masekela - Rejoice; Kokoroko - Could We Be More

note: The Mizell Brothers make jazz-funk that sounds designed for a future crate-digger, and Blue Note's biggest seller resulted.
listen_for: Harvey Mason's clean, unswung backbeat under all that harmony.

note: Slow, warm, spacious, and endlessly sampled: the template for jazz as atmosphere.
listen_for: How little the drums do, and how much that little does.

note: The record where jazz drumming, studio perfectionism, and pop songwriting fuse completely. Purdie and Gadd on the same album, doing opposite things.
listen_for: The half-time shuffle on "Home at Last"; Gadd unravelling the title track.
connections: Steely Dan - Gaucho; Paul Simon - Still Crazy After All These Years

note: Longer, colder, more expensive, and home to "Babylon Sisters" — arguably the definitive recorded Purdie shuffle.
listen_for: Ghost notes so quiet you feel them as swing rather than hear them as hits.

note: The rawest of the trio, where the session players still sound like a band having an argument.
listen_for: Drums pushing the tempo when the arrangement refuses to.

album: Still Crazy After All These Years
note: Steve Gadd's "50 Ways" pattern is one of the few drum parts non-drummers can hum.
listen_for: A marching rudiment repurposed as a pop hook.

note: Mike Clark's "Actual Proof" is the linear-funk summit: a groove that never repeats and never loses the pocket.
listen_for: Every limb playing a separate voice with no note doubled.
connections: Snarky Puppy - We Like It Here

note: Fusion at its most melodic, with a rhythm section that swings despite the technology.
listen_for: How the drums stay out of Jaco's way while still driving everything.

note: Lenny White's precision-engineered complexity — the maximalist wing of the tradition.
listen_for: Odd-metre passages played as if they were natural dance rhythms.

note: The New York session elite as their own band, with two drummers and nothing to prove to a producer.
listen_for: Steve Gadd and Chris Parker sharing one groove without collision.

note: The crate-digger's Rosetta Stone: sophisticated fusion carrying breaks that hip-hop would later build on wholesale.
listen_for: The percussion break in "Take Me to the Mardi Gras", later the spine of "Peter Piper".

note: "Talkin' All That Jazz" argues the case for sampling as a musical practice, on record, before the courts got involved.
listen_for: A live-band hip-hop group defending the loop with a loop.

note: The record that fixed the relationship between jazz and hip-hop for the next thirty years. Minimal, warm, and rhythmically immaculate.
listen_for: Upright bass and a dry drum loop with almost nothing else in the frame.
connections: A Tribe Called Quest - Midnight Marauders; The Roots - Do You Want More?!!!??!

note: Denser and funkier, with the group's sample choices sharpened into a house style.
listen_for: The swing on the drums, always slightly behind the rap cadence.
connections: Pete Rock & CL Smooth - Mecca and the Soul Brother

note: The most luxurious drum programming of the era: horns, filtered bass, and breaks that hit like a live room.
listen_for: Snares layered until they thud rather than crack.

note: DJ Premier's stripped, percussive chops treat jazz records as rhythm sources rather than melodies.
listen_for: Drum loops so dry they sound like a room with the carpet pulled up.

album: Reachin' (A New Refutation of Time and Space)
note: Cool-jazz atmosphere as a whole worldview, complete with upright bass and brushed-snare softness.
listen_for: Loops chosen for their air rather than their impact.

note: Rather than sample the players, hire them: Donald Byrd, Roy Ayers, and Lonnie Liston Smith in the room.
listen_for: Live drums recorded to sit inside a hip-hop mix rather than above it.

note: Blue Note licenses its own archive to a hip-hop project, and the loop is formally legitimised.
listen_for: Hard-bop drum breaks used as pop hooks.

note: Questlove plays the loop instead of sampling it, and the live band re-enters the story.
listen_for: Human repetition maintained with machine discipline.

note: UK acid jazz meets American rappers, and the transatlantic thread that leads to broken beat opens.
listen_for: Band-played breaks engineered to feel sampled.

note: Drum and bass programmers write for strings and jazz harmony, and broken beat's blueprint appears.
section: 1997-2006: the producer sits behind the kit
listen_for: Rhythms that swing and stumble in the same bar.
connections: Bugz in the Attic - Back in the Doghouse; Jazzanova - In Between

note: The most important rhythm record of its decade: a band playing deliberately, audibly late and never losing the pocket.
section: 1997-2006: the producer sits behind the kit
listen_for: Snare consistently behind the bass, creating an almost drunken lean.
connections: Erykah Badu - Mama's Gun; Robert Glasper Experiment - Black Radio

note: The same rhythm section applied to songwriting, and the proof that the technique could carry hooks.
section: 1997-2006: the producer sits behind the kit
listen_for: Drums that breathe with the vocal rather than under it.

note: Ninja Tune's jazz wing: live drums recorded for depth, then edited with a producer's ear.
section: 1997-2006: the producer sits behind the kit
listen_for: Loops assembled from a real kit, then left to run past the point of comfort.

note: Norwegian post-rock precision applied to a jazz big band, with rhythm as the organising principle.
section: 1997-2006: the producer sits behind the kit
listen_for: Programmed and acoustic percussion made deliberately indistinguishable.

note: Blue Note hands its vaults to a producer, who reassembles the label as a beat record.
section: 1997-2006: the producer sits behind the kit
listen_for: Drums re-chopped so the original session players become sidemen to the loop.

note: Broken beat's European wing, elegant and rhythmically restless.
section: 1997-2006: the producer sits behind the kit
listen_for: The bar that never quite resolves where you expect.

note: Roy Hargrove builds a band around the neo-soul groove, formally joining jazz to the Dilla lineage.
section: 1997-2006: the producer sits behind the kit
listen_for: Horn writing that defers entirely to the rhythm section.

note: The American organ-trio route into the same territory, with turntables and dub space.
section: 1997-2006: the producer sits behind the kit
listen_for: Billy Martin playing textures where a groove is expected.

note: The West London collective's statement album, and broken beat at its most physical.
section: 1997-2006: the producer sits behind the kit
listen_for: Syncopation dense enough to disguise where "one" is.

note: The source code. Unquantised drum programming turned into a compositional method, assembled largely from a hospital bed.
listen_for: Hits that land early or late and are unmistakably intentional.
connections: Karriem Riggins - Alone Together; Robert Glasper Experiment - Black Radio

note: Chris Dave performs the sampler's imperfection live, and jazz's institutions finally give it a prize.
listen_for: The hi-hat pattern deliberately fighting the snare placement.

note: A working jazz drummer making a beat tape, collapsing the two disciplines into one person.
listen_for: Short sketches that stop before they become songs, on purpose.

note: The Toronto trio's first album of originals, and the moment the covers band becomes a serious rhythm outfit.
listen_for: Alexander Sowinski playing hip-hop weight with jazz-trio interplay.

note: Spiritual jazz returns at maximum scale, with two drummers and a rhythmic density that owes as much to LA beat culture as to Coltrane.
listen_for: Two kits locking and diverging across a three-hour album.

note: Live improvisation edited into loops: the producer's technique applied to a drummer's own performance.
listen_for: Seams where the edit happens, left audible as a statement.

note: The technical wing, and a reminder that this lineage also contains people who simply want to play very hard, very accurately.
listen_for: Robert Searight's pocket holding steady under absurd arrangements.

note: An acoustic trio playing electronic rhythms without triggers, translating breakbeats onto a kit.
listen_for: Rob Turner reproducing programmed subdivisions by hand.

note: Brad Mehldau and Mark Guiliana as a two-person band where the drums are the lead instrument.
listen_for: Guiliana's electronic-derived phrasing played entirely acoustically.

note: The LA beat scene's most ambitious record, and the bridge between Dilla's grid and free jazz's chaos.
listen_for: Rhythms that shatter mid-track and reassemble.

note: Melbourne's answer: neo-soul harmony with metric modulation treated as a pop device.
listen_for: Perrin Moss changing the feel underneath a chorus without warning.
connections: Tom Misch & Yussef Dayes - What Kinda Music

note: The record that opened the current London scene to the world, cut fast and loose by a drummer and a keyboardist.
listen_for: Dayes' ride cymbal doing the work a synth would do elsewhere.
connections: Yussef Dayes - Black Classical Music; Tom Misch & Yussef Dayes - What Kinda Music

note: Twin drum kits, tuba bass, and Caribbean carnival rhythm reframing what a jazz group can be.
listen_for: Two drummers deliberately refusing to lock together.
connections: Ezra Collective - Where I'm Meant to Be

note: A drummer producing his own record, with grime, Afrobeat, and dub given equal weight to jazz.
listen_for: Programmed and played drums layered until the boundary vanishes.

note: Femi Koleoso leads from the kit, and a joyful, danceable jazz record wins the Mercury Prize.
listen_for: Afrobeat and reggae feels swapped mid-tune without a seam.

note: Four cities, four bands, one editor: the method from In the Moment scaled up into a statement.
listen_for: The consistency of feel across completely different rooms.

note: The trio drop the vocal features and make an instrumental record with orchestral arrangements, Arthur Verocai included.
listen_for: Sowinski's drums given the space of a jazz record rather than a beat tape.

note: A drummer's solo album conceived as a career statement, spanning Afrobeat, fusion, and spiritual jazz.
listen_for: Fills that behave like melodies rather than punctuation.

note: The crossover record: bedroom-pop production meeting a drummer who will not simplify.
listen_for: Complex drumming mixed like a pop record and none the worse for it.

note: London's Afrobeat inheritors, taking the Tony Allen lineage first-hand rather than second.
listen_for: Percussion and kit sharing one pulse in Allen's manner.

note: Recorded years earlier, released posthumously for both: the origin of Afrobeat drumming meeting South African jazz.
listen_for: An eighty-year-old playing with more space than anyone half his age.

note: The internet-native extreme: absurd precision, cartoon energy, and a drummer playing figures that read as programmed.
listen_for: Micro-timing so exact it loops back around to sounding synthetic.

note: Richmond, Virginia's answer, where the band swaps between jazz, hip-hop, and funk without announcing it.
listen_for: Corey Fonville switching feel every eight bars.
